Author: @m.h.w.weckseler
Content:
1:15 As someone who uses 'cut resistant gloves' daily in a factory setting, i have several issues with this.
First, the name is cut resistant; not stab proof. Even a (standard) kevlar vest is not stab proof.
Second, it's cut resistant, not cut proof. It resists cutting not stop it.
Third. They are mostly meant to prevent small cuts you would get from handling glass, or in my case sharp metal edges as you work with it.
Forth, again, it's resistant. The point is that by the time you do indeed feel a cut, you should have already stopped doing what made the cut.
And fifth, we once tested leader gloves and they lasted exactly 20 seconds before the palm (of the glove) was cut wide open. The cut resistant gloves we use at work last me 2-3 8 hour shifts before small holes starts forming. Which is also the moment you throw them away and get new ones.
And i think that's enough 'but no' for now.

You have to keep in mind that the sun moves. 

You let it sit out in the sun for 3 hours as if that was going to heat up the pan more. 

You need to line up the dot like you did at the beginning. Then keep moving it every 10 minutes or so. By the time 3 hours had rolled along, the sun would have been completely out of alignment.  

For best results you want to also use it midday. 

Ideally when you get a new piece of equipment you should consult with somebody who has successfully used it.

Content:
CUT-resistant does not mean STAB-resistant.
Notice the signficantly different spelling there?
Stabbing applies a completely different pressure to a much smaller point than when cutting.
So applying stabbing force to cut-resistant gloves is like complaining about a flamethrower not being able to slow-cook something. Similar general ideas, highly different application.

Edit: I don't know if the gloves Guga picked up are somehow different to the ones I own, but mine have prevented some serious cuts even with my professionally sharpened Santoku knives. No, they don't prevent ALL cuts but they at least give the required amount of protection to prevent a deep cut. Shrug, maybe different products; just my guess.

Author: @Alan_Howell
Content:
The solar cooker will work if you move it every 15 minutes or so to track the Sun. Reflecting (and concentrating) solar cookers DO get hot...far, far hotter than most ovens. I have two that will get between 700-900F very quickly and likely much hotter because it maxes out my thermocouple. (See my channel for solar cooking examples). 

But the main point of solar cookers is that they use zero electrical or fossil fuel, no firewood, etc. You can cook on any sunny day, free, albeit they just take more time. They have special applications for areas that cannot have fires, or lack proper (or legal) firewood. It uses zero electricity or fuel since it works by nuclear fusion (ie the Sun). I cook with solar cookers of all styles and they are great for specific applications/areas.

Content: The egg cracker is for soft boilled eggs not for raw eggs. It is for 'oeuf à la coque' and you need a 'coquetier' (an egg cup)'. And no you don't get salmonella from it , because it is used in countries with strict food regulation where you can keep your eggs at room temperature for 30 days. Unlike in the US where eggs have their natural protective coating removed and the egg bleached.

Author: @hervevazeilles3790
Content: Protective gloves have mecanical protection ratings. EN388 rating is a shield with numbers underneath each number is a different test rating from 0 to 5. In order they are abrasion, cut, tear, puncture. Anything below 5 for cut and punture, will not resist a sharp kitchen knife. It is mainly aimed at protecting your hand when working with sharpish objects like sheet metal, raw metal pieces. For butchering gloves you want chainmail gloves.

If you want a charcoal flavor, follow these steps:
 1- Place the meat in a pan, ensuring enough space between slices.
 2- Use a small cup and add oil with a high smoke point.

 4- Carefully place the hot charcoal in the cup of oil.
 5- Let it sit for a few minutes until the charcoal stops burning.

  Warnings:
 •  Do not use this method multiple times a month.
 •  Do not inhale the smoke. (you might pass out)

Author: @tildessmoo
Content:
The aluminum defrosting... tray? pan? sheet? whatever, it actually does defrost a little faster than just leaving something out on the counter, because aluminum conducts heat, and the tray has more surface area than the sorts of things you usually put on it, so it can conduct the energy from, say, 2.5 square feet of air surface into the 2/3 square foot surface of the food touching it. It's nowhere near as fast as putting something in a bowl of water, because, while water is less conductive than aluminum, it has a _much_ higher specific heat, meaning it can transfer more energy into whatever you're defrosting before its temperature lowers (and temperature difference is what determines energy transfer), plus, being a liquid, it has basically infinite surface area in contact with whatever you're defrosting. However, both of these methods rely on only one method of energy transfer: conduction. If you combine methods of energy transfer (the three main ones being: conduction, radiation, and convection), you can defrost even faster. Now, increasing radiation transfer without cooking anything is a tricky proposition in the home, but you can add convection to the bowl of water by putting the bowl under a running faucet.

Seriously, just put your vacuum-packed steak in a bowl in the sink, turn on the cold water, and let it run. It'll defrost so quickly even the still-water bowl method will look slow in comparison.
